keyAndScale.keySignature: No sharps or flats (C major key signature; G Mixolydian is the 5th mode of C major)
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: E minor (relative minor of G major)

mainProgression.description: A 12-bar blues variation in 6/4 time using dominant 7th chords throughout, with the distinctive chromatic turnaround using D7#9 to Eb7#9 and back

sectionProgressions.description: Four bars of G7 establishing the tonic dominant quality with the signature riff played by the horns
Standard blues IV chord movement; guitar comps with C7 voicings shifting the tonal center briefly
Return to the G7 tonic area before the turnaround
The distinctive chromatic turnaround featuring the #9 voicings that give All Blues its unique harmonic identity

harmonicFunction: G7 (I7) - Tonic dominant chord; the Mixolydian home base creates a suspended, floating quality
C7 (IV7) - Subdominant providing classic blues movement away from the tonic
D7#9 (V7#9) - Dominant chord with the Hendrix chord quality creating strong pull to resolve
Eb7#9 (bVI7#9) - Chromatic upper neighbor to D7#9, creating the signature half-step chromatic slide
The 6/4 time signature creates a waltz-like feel that distinguishes this from standard 4/4 blues
The #9 voicings (containing both major and minor 3rds) are essential to the jazz-blues character

techniques.name: Jazz Comping with Dominant 7th Voicings
techniques.description: Accompanying the ensemble using compact dominant 7th chord voicings with rhythmic variation, providing harmonic support while leaving space for soloists

notes: G7: 3-2-0-0-0-1 (open voicing) or X-10-12-10-12-X (closed voicing)
C7: X-3-2-3-1-0 (open) or 8-10-8-9-8-X (closed voicing at 8th fret)
D7#9: X-5-4-5-5-X (the Hendrix chord voicing at 5th fret)
Eb7#9: X-6-5-6-6-X (same shape shifted up one fret)
Use 3-note and 4-note voicings on the middle strings to stay out of the bass register
Rhythmic comping should be sparse and syncopated, not on every beat
sequence: Establish the G7 comp pattern using a swing feel in 6/4
Play on beats 2, 4, and 6 (or varied syncopations) to avoid clashing with bass
Shift voicings up a fret for Eb7#9 from D7#9 position
Leave space during solos - comping should breathe
Follow the form: 4 bars G7, 2 bars C7, 2 bars G7, turnaround
tips: Less is more - jazz comping leaves generous space for the soloist
Use a clean or very lightly overdriven tone for warmth
Practice the 12-bar form until you can follow it without thinking
Listen to Freddie Green or Jim Hall for jazz comping style references
Swing the eighth notes: long-short feel rather than even eighths

techniques.name: Chord Extensions and Alterations
techniques.description: Using extended and altered chord tones (9ths, 13ths, #9) to create sophisticated jazz harmony beyond basic triads and seventh chords

notes: G9: 3-X-0-2-0-1 or X-10-9-10-10-X (adds the 9th/A note)
G13: 3-X-0-0-0-0 (open strings create the 13th/E) or 3-X-2-4-3-X
C9: X-3-2-3-3-3 (adds the 9th/D note to C7)
D7#9: The #9 (E#/F natural) creates tension needing resolution
Eb7#9: Same structure as D7#9 shifted up a half step
Mix basic 7th voicings with extended voicings for variety
sequence: Start with basic dominant 7th voicings to learn the form
Gradually substitute extended voicings (9ths, 13ths) for color
Practice the D7#9 to Eb7#9 chromatic slide as a consistent gesture
Experiment with different voicing inversions for smooth voice leading
Combine basic and extended voicings within a single chorus
tips: Learn multiple voicings for each chord at different neck positions
Prioritize smooth voice leading - move as few notes as possible between chords
The #9 voicing is the defining sound of this turnaround - master it
Practice switching between G7, G9, and G13 voicings to add variety
Keep your voicings in the middle register to blend with the ensemble

techniques.name: 6/4 Swing Feel
techniques.description: Internalizing the 6/4 time signature with a jazz swing feel, which gives All Blues its distinctive waltz-like groove distinctly different from standard 4/4 blues

notes: 6/4 time = 6 quarter-note beats per measure
Can be felt as two groups of 3 (waltz in 2) or three groups of 2
All Blues primarily uses a feel of two groups of 3 (ONE-two-three-FOUR-five-six)
Swing the subdivisions: eighth notes are played with a long-short triplet feel
Jimmy Cobb's brushwork on drums defines the groove - listen to it carefully
sequence: Count 1-2-3-4-5-6 while tapping foot on 1 and 4
Practice comping on beats 2, 4, and 6 with swing feel
Clap the rhythm before adding chord voicings
Play along with the recording focusing on locking with the drums
Practice the 12-bar form cycling continuously in 6/4
tips: Donthe iconic vocal hookstrange' - just feel the waltz groove
Listen to the original recording repeatedly to absorb the feel
Practice with a slow metronome set to dotted half notes (2 clicks per bar)
The bass walks in a 6/4 pattern - use it as your rhythmic anchor
Relax into the groove rather than counting rigidly
details.progression: Applies to the entire song form

sections.name: Intro/Vamp
sections.description: Piano and bass establish the 6/4 groove with the signature two-note riff (G and Ab oscillation) before the head melody enters. Guitar should comp lightly or lay out.
notes: The opening vamp is primarily piano and bass - guitar can lay out
If comping, use sparse G7 voicings on beats 4-6 only
The G-Ab auxiliary note figure in the bass defines the piece
Establish the 6/4 feel before the head melody enters

sections.name: Head (Theme)
sections.description: The melody (head) is played by Miles Davis on trumpet. Guitar provides supportive comping using the 12-bar form with sparse, rhythmically varied voicings.
notes: Support the trumpet melody with light comping
Follow the 12-bar form precisely
The turnaround (D7#9 - Eb7#9 - D7#9) is the harmonic highlight
Keep volume low during the head to let the melody sing

sections.name: Solo Section (Miles Davis)
sections.description: Miles Davis solos over the form. Guitar maintains light, supportive comping, following the harmonic form and responding to the soloist's phrasing.
notes: Comp responsively - react to what the soloist plays
Leave plenty of space between chord hits
Vary your voicings and rhythms each chorus to keep it fresh
The form repeats multiple times - maintain concentration through each chorus

sections.name: Solo Section (Cannonball Adderley / Coltrane)
sections.description: Saxophone solos over the form. This section presents opportunity for more adventurous comping, using extended voicings and varied rhythmic patterns.
notes: Use more adventurous voicings as the energy builds through solos
Extended chords (9ths, 13ths) add harmonic interest during longer solo sections
Balance increased harmonic activity with continued restraint
Follow the soloist's energy level with your comping intensity

sections.name: Head Out (Final Theme)
sections.description: Return of the head melody to close the performance. Comping returns to the restrained approach of the opening head.
notes: Return to the sparse comping style of the opening head
Match the dynamic of the ensemble winding down
The turnaround chords should be played with finality
Let the melody be the primary focus again

sections.name: Outro/Vamp
sections.description: Return to the opening vamp figure, gradually fading as the ensemble winds down the performance.
notes: Return to the two-note vamp figure from the intro
Gradually reduce comping as the piece fades
Match the ensemble's diminuendo
The piece ends quietly on the G7 vamp

guitar.recommended: Archtop hollow-body guitar (Gibson L-5, ES-175, or similar)
alternatives: Any semi-hollow or hollow-body with warm pickups
guitar.pickup: Neck humbucker for warm, round jazz tone with rolled-off treble

amp.recommended: Fender Twin Reverb or similar clean amp

effects.reverb: Light spring or room reverb for natural ambience
effects.other: No effects needed; pure clean tone is the jazz standard

beginner.focus: Learn the 12-bar blues form and basic dominant 7th chord shapes
steps: Learn open G7 and C7 chord voicings
Strum through the form slowly with basic voicings
Listen to the original recording repeatedly to absorb the feel

intermediate.focus: Develop jazz comping technique and master the turnaround voicings
steps: Learn D7#9 and Eb7#9 chord voicings (Hendrix chord shapes)
Practice the chromatic turnaround slide between D7#9 and Eb7#9
Develop a swing feel in 6/4 time with syncopated comping
Learn multiple voicings for G7 and C7 across the neck
Practice comping along with the recording following the form

advanced.focus: Master extended voicings, responsive comping, and improvisation over the form
steps: Use 9th, 13th, and altered voicings for harmonic variety
Develop responsive comping that reacts to the soloist
Begin improvising melodies over the 12-bar form using Mixolydian and blues scales
Practice with a metronome and backing tracks at various tempos
Perform with other musicians in a jazz combo setting
advanced.timeEstimate: 2-4 months for performance-ready comping and soloing

commonMistakes: Overplaying - comping too frequently and not leaving space for the soloist
Playing in 4/4 feel instead of the correct 6/4 waltz-like groove
Using rock-style power chords instead of jazz 7th chord voicings
Swinging too aggressively or not swinging at all (playing straight eighths)
Losing track of the 12-bar form during extended solo sections
practiceRoutine: Warm up with dominant 7th chord voicings in multiple positions for 5 minutes
Count through the 12-bar form in 6/4 while tapping the swing groove
Practice the turnaround (D7#9 - Eb7#9 - D7#9 - G7) as an isolated loop
Comp through the entire form with the recording for at least 3 full cycles
Practice improvising a simple melody using the G Mixolydian and G blues scales
focusAreas: Internalizing the 6/4 time feel with swing
Smooth voice leading between chord changes
The D7#9 to Eb7#9 chromatic turnaround voicing
Dynamic and rhythmic variety in comping
Knowing the 12-bar form automatically without counting bars
metronomeWork: Set metronome to dotted half notes for 2 beats per 6/4 measure (about 46 BPM per click)
Practice comping on offbeats while metronome clicks on 1 and 4
Gradually increase from 100 BPM to 138 BPM in quarter notes
Practice the form with just beats 1 and 4 sounding to test independence
Use a swing-eighth metronome setting if available for authentic feel
